why: A record of how this fleet's failures are actually worded. Stado shells out to ssh, rsync, gcloud, curl, launchctl and a dozen HTTP clients, and by the time an error reaches this crate it is prose. These lists are not a guess at English: each family is a set of spellings that were observed coming back from those tools, and the order they are tested in is load-bearing — a wrong order sent an operator to the credential vault for what was a chmod. Kept as data, with the reason for each family and for its position, so that adding a spelling is adding a line to a record rather than editing a classifier nobody can read. Order of evaluation is the order of the families below.

families.name: config
families.why: A missing or malformed environment variable is our outage, not the operator's mistake — and neither is a tool we never installed on the box. Tested first: these sentences often also contain the word 'not found', which would otherwise claim them.

notes.be configured: doctor's release row says 'must all be configured', and the same shape reaches here as 'must be configured'. Matching the phrase rather than the negation keeps a broken configuration out of unknown.

families.name: ssh_auth
families.why: SSH's own refusal is a credential failure however it is spelled around a path, and it must keep winning over the filesystem reading below.

families.name: filesystem_refusal
families.why: A file or directory the host itself would not open. The words overlap with the auth family — `find: /x: Permission denied` and an object gateway's `permission denied` are spelled the same — but the meaning does not: no credential of ours was rejected, and telling the operator 'retrying will not help, check your credentials' sends them to the vault for a chmod. On 2026-09-17 `stado space report lukasz-macbook` did exactly that over one unreadable Google Drive .tmp. Checked before the auth needles and landed in unknown with the detail intact, because the seven-code vocabulary has no code for 'the host refused a file operation' and inventing one here is not this crate's call.

families.name: auth
families.why: A credential of ours was rejected: retrying will not help until it is replaced.

families.name: rate_limit
families.why: Ours to wait out, exactly like a dead dependency.

families.name: timeout
families.why: The operation did not answer in time; the work may still be running on the far side.

families.name: network
families.why: Transport-level failures. Every HTTP client words these differently, and the wording is all we get once the error has been flattened to a string.

families.name: not_found
families.why: A resource the operator named that does not exist. Checked last among the needles: 'not found' is a substring of far too many sentences that are really about something else, `command not found` being the worst of them.

upstream_status_why: Most of this fleet's failures arrive as prose that has an HTTP status embedded in it — `GCS API error HTTP 503: ...`, `... -> HTTP 429: ...`. That status is real structured evidence and beats any keyword, so it is read before the families above are tried.
